paras: The pursuit of James Wilson was an incident on the night of August 23, 1900, in Chicago, Illinois, in which a street crowd chased Wilson, a Black ventriloquist, after mistaking the rag doll he used in his act for a white child he had kidnapped. Wilson escaped unhurt on a street car, and newspapers reported the episode as "a narrow escape from lynching."

Wilson performed on street corners and, to draw an audience, held what looked like a white infant but was a rag baby. According to the St. Louis Republic and the Polish-language Dziennik Chicagoski, he set up that evening at the corner of Noble and Blackhawk streets.

The doll seemed to cry: a wire dispatch said Wilson "threw his voice" into it, while the St. Louis Republic said he shook it until it wailed. A woman, described by the Republic as "nearsighted," took the doll for a real white child in distress and raised the alarm that Wilson was a kidnapper. Dziennik Chicagoski wrote that she cried out to passers-by that the Negro was carrying off a white child.

Wilson ran, and a crowd that the Republic put at "half a hundred" and the Chicago paper at several dozen went after him. In the wire version the pursuers shouted "Kill him, Lynch him; he is a kidnapper." With the crowd close behind him on North Ashland avenue, he jumped onto a street car, and the conductor kept the pursuers off, by the Republic's account by "vigorously flourishing a controlling lever." The Republic added that Wilson threw the rag baby at the crowd and sat down to catch his breath.
No report of an arrest, injury or police action appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers through three separately written reports. A Chicago wire dispatch dated August 24 ran that day in the Alexandria Gazette as "A Narrow Escape" and on August 25 in Colorado's Daily Sentinel as "Narrow Escape From Lynching," quoting the crowd's cries and calling Wilson "the fleeing negro." The St. Louis Republic printed its own special under "Mob Thought Negro Was Beating White Baby" and played it for laughs, crediting Wilson's survival to "a pair of long, speedy legs" and calling the doll "the ink-faced child." The same piece remarked that "it looked for a few moments as if there would be another negro riot."

In Chicago itself, Dziennik Chicagoski ran the item on August 24 under "Niewinnie scigany" ("Innocently pursued"), saying Wilson had been suspected unjustly, though through his own fault. By August 31 the story had shrunk to a single line in Mississippi's Southern Herald, which dropped the lynching language and said only that he "narrowly escaped rough treatment." No coverage in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Pursuit of James Wilson (Chicago, 1900)
bases: A crowd chased Wilson as a supposed kidnapper, shouting 'Kill him, Lynch him' in the wire version, and the papers called it a narrow escape from lynching; no one was hurt (A1, A3).

A street crowd of dozens pursued Wilson on a kidnapping suspicion and, in the wire version, cried for his lynching, but he escaped on a street car and no one was killed or reported injured (A1, A2, A3); it was a threatened lynching, not a completed one.

Three independently written reports, a wire dispatch (A1), the St. Louis Republic's own special (A3) and a local Chicago Polish-language daily (A2), agree on the core event: Wilson, a Black ventriloquist, was mistaken for a kidnapper and chased by a crowd.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Wilson 'threw his voice' into a rag baby that looked like a white infant; a woman leaped toward him and a crowd chased him shouting 'Kill him, Lynch him; he is a kidnapper' until he escaped on a street car with the conductor's help.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republic special
accounts.gist: Wilson shook the 'baby' so that it wailed; a nearsighted woman thought he was mistreating a white child and cried 'He's a kidnaper', and about fifty people chased him along North Ashland avenue until a conductor held them off with a lever; Wilson threw the rag baby at his pursuers.

accounts.label: Dziennik Chicagoski (local Polish-language daily)
accounts.gist: A doll in a shawl seemed to cry, a woman alerted passers-by that the Negro was carrying off a white child, and several dozen people rushed at him; unable to explain himself, he fled (the text breaks off).

framing.detail: Headlines 'A Narrow Escape' and 'Narrow Escape From Lynching'; the dispatch quotes the crowd's cries and calls Wilson 'the fleeing negro'.

The St. Louis Republic played the chase for laughs ('a pair of long, speedy legs', 'the ink-faced child', 'break all sprinting records') under 'Mob Thought Negro Was Beating White Baby' and remarked that there nearly was 'another negro riot'.
Dziennik Chicagoski headed it 'Niewinnie scigany' (Innocently pursued) and said the suspicion was unjust, though brought on by his own fault.
The Southern Herald reduced it to one line among news briefs, saying he 'narrowly escaped rough treatment'.

info: The night of Aug. 23, 1900 ('last night' in dispatches dated Aug. 24; 'Wczoraj' [yesterday] in the Aug. 24 local paper)
Street corner at Noble and Blackhawk streets, Chicago; the chase ran along Blackhawk street and, per the St. Louis Republic, North Ashland avenue
James Wilson, described as 'a negro ventriloquist'
Suspected of kidnapping (or mistreating) a white child, when the 'baby' he held was a rag doll
A street crowd raised by a woman's cry; the papers do not state the crowd's race or name anyone
Wilson boarded a street car and the conductor kept the crowd back, by 'vigorously flourishing a controlling lever' per the St. Louis Republic
